article_title: Future Forward Literacy
citation: Future Forward: Evidence Rating Strong program description. (2022). https://www.evidenceforlearners.org/future-forward
title: School-community-family partnership pattern pairing tutoring dosage with regular family contact
description: The program's design pattern combines a minimum tutoring dosage with structured family outreach: "FF sites are expected to provide students with a minimum of three 30-minute tutoring sessions per week and to communicate with families at least two times per month." Tutoring is individualized, with sessions varying "based on the skills and interests of the students," while the family engagement coordinator runs monthly family events and ongoing contacts to support literacy development outside school.

A family engagement coordinator for family outreach and communication
Generally paraprofessional tutors conducting one-on-one sessions

article_title: TeachArena: Are Language Agents Ready for Realistic Teaching Work?
citation: Zixin Chen, Peng Liu, Rui Sheng, Haobo Li, Jianhong Tu, Xiaodong Deng, Kashun Shum, Dayiheng Liu, Huamin Qu. (2026). Are Agents Ready to Teach? A Multi-Stage Benchmark for Real-World Teaching Workflows. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14322
title: Deploy tutor agents as bounded delegates that retain supporting evidence, expose changes, verify state, and seek approval when evidence or authority is insufficient
description: The article recommends that once agents can grade, revise materials, or contact students, deployment should treat them as bounded operational delegates: "consequential actions should retain their supporting evidence, expose what was changed and why, verify the resulting state, and seek approval when evidence or authority is insufficient." This follows from the finding that low performance on long-chain workflows is consistent with a gap between producing plausible local actions and completing a warranted institutional intervention. The article argues greater autonomy without these properties would expand the consequences of an error rather than the agent's teaching capability.
requirements: Consequential actions must retain supporting evidence and expose what was changed and why
The resulting state must be verified, with approval sought when evidence or authority is insufficient
constraints: The article states TeachArena does not determine which architecture is best, only that it enables testing whether systems become more learning-oriented without becoming less operationally reliable
target_learners: frontier language models deployed as tutor agents in institutional settings
target_learning_goals: preserving educational rationale across institutional workflows
accountability and privacy in automated teaching actions
examples: The MM-04 verifier stack requires querying historical submissions before computation, deck inspection before editing, computation before material design, and completed materials before announcement

article_title: The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks
citation: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22687
title: 24-task set derived from the Taxonomy of User Needs and Actions (TUNA) with easy and difficult variants
description: The article constructed a set of 24 tasks "derived from the Taxonomy of User Needs and Actions (TUNA), a framework of different ways that people use AI based on different degrees of cognitive effort required." The tasks span TUNA's four categories — information seeking, information processing and synthesis, procedural guidance and execution, and content creation and transformation — with three task types per category and an easy and difficult variant per task (e.g., naming one versus five Olympic medalists). All tasks were completable in under five minutes independently and were used across the three studies with a GPT-4o chat interface.
requirements: Tasks are drawn from TUNA's four cognitively distinct categories with easy and difficult variants per task type
constraints: All tasks are relatively simple and can be completed in under five minutes independently
target_learners: Adult crowdworkers completing simple cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: Measuring AI-use choices, completion time, and mental effort on simple cognitive tasks
examples: Example easy tasks include "Name the color that you get when you mix white and black" and "Calculate: 27 + 56"; difficult variants extend the same task types.

article_title: Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI
citation: Zara Contractor and Germán Reyes. (2026). Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08849
title: A model of learning with AI in which AI acts as a tutor that raises the return to research effort or as a delegate that replaces the student's own writing
description: The article builds a model in which a student divides cognitive effort between research (reading and searching) and writing, both producing knowledge, with writing also producing the essay. The article states: "We model AI as a technology that gives the student two non-mutually exclusive capabilities" — used as a tutor it raises the return to research effort, and used to write the essay it lets the student delegate, removing the essay-quality reward from the student's own work so effort falls in both activities. The model rationalizes the test-score gain, the time shift from writing toward research, and the enjoyment gain, and predicts that outcomes differ by use type.
requirements: Students choose how to use AI; the model treats delegation as a choice variable whose threshold rises with the value the student places on knowledge
constraints: The model is an organizing framework the authors use to rationalize their experimental results, not an independently estimated structural model in the main text; the complete model is in Appendix D
target_learners: undergraduates completing time-bounded academic assignments on unfamiliar topics
target_learning_goals: factual and conceptual knowledge acquisition and retention
analytical essay writing
examples: The model's prediction that delegated essays' quality advantage should vanish once AI is removed is examined with the Session Two unaided essays

citation: Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, and Baichuan Li. (2026). Beyond Helpfulness: A Teaching-over-Solving Diagnostic for Measuring Educational Impact in LLM Tutors. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16206

The article analyzes its rubric metadata with a deterministic label mapping to measure agency-dimension and agency-skill density, finding one representative criterion requires the tutor to "provide hint[s] ... by asking at least 2 guiding questions without completely showing next steps."

target_learning_goals: evaluating tutoring behavior against agency-preserving pedagogical criteria

article_title: Informal Learning Emerges in Everyday Human-LLM Interaction
citation: Chen, Z., Li, H., Xiao, Z., Qu, H., & Xie, X. (2026). Informal learning emerges in everyday human–LLM interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17643
title: Turn-level behavioural signatures of informal learning: ICAP engagement depth and scaffolding translated into role-specific labels for naturalistic human–LLM logs
description: The article translates learning-science constructs into role-specific, turn-level behavioural signatures for naturalistic logs: user turns are coded by engagement depth (passive, active, constructive, drawing on the ICAP framework), and assistant turns by whether they deliver requested content or provide scaffolded support, further characterized by support intent (metacognitive, cognitive, affective) and support form (feedback, hinting, instructing, explaining, modelling, questioning). The framework states that "Labels indicate observable learning-oriented participation, not durable learning outcomes or causal instructional effects." It supports analyses of engagement presence, contextual organization and support–engagement coupling at conversation-level, support-form and adjacent-turn scales.
requirements: Requires theory-grounded codebook development, independent human review, prompt calibration and corpus-scale LLM-assisted labelling of turns, as described in the annotation workflow
constraints: Labels are behavioural indicators rather than direct evidence of retention, transfer or skill development
The ICAP interactive category is not used as a turn-level user label because every record is already a human–assistant exchange
target_learners: Adult everyday users of general-purpose LLM assistants in coding and writing tasks
target_learning_goals: Observable learning-oriented participation during everyday task-focused human–LLM problem solving
examples: Applied to 128,569 conversations from WildChat, LMSYS Chat and ShareChat, yielding 491,685 user turns and 489,785 assistant turns coded at three scales

article_title: Regulating the AI Tutor: Intentions, Help-Seeking, and Self-Regulated Learning in Adolescent GenAI Use
citation: Rania Abdelghani, Peter Kaiser, and Kou Murayama. (2026). Regulating the AI Tutor: Intentions, Help-Seeking, and Self-Regulated Learning in Adolescent GenAI Use. Accepted at the NextGen Learning Interfaces Workshop, AIED 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08568
title: Turn-level coding framework combining SRL, help-seeking, and mathematical modeling codes with LLM-specific constructs of epistemic vigilance and agency over the AI
description: The article proposes a hybrid turn-level coding framework applied to each task-relevant student turn in AI-tutor conversations. Deductive codes follow Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model (PLAN, MONITOR, REQUEST, EVALUATE), with REQUEST turns further coded as instrumental or executive and by content type, plus a Blum-based modeling-process code. Two inductive LLM-specific constructs were derived via an exploratory pass with Gemini 2.5 Pro: "Epistemic vigilance is a three-valued code (not_applicable, caught, missed) capturing whether a student reacts to an inaccurate or mismatched AI turn", and a binary "Agency over the AI" marker capturing attempts to shape the AI's role, format, or scaffolding.
requirements: Task-relevant student turns from AI-tutor chat logs; a stratified human-validation pass by domain experts to establish per-construct reliability
constraints: Behavioral analyses currently rely on AI coding alone; human validation is ongoing
Derived from an exploratory pass on a randomly selected 30% of conversations
target_learners: adolescent secondary-school students (Grade 9, ages 14-15)
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and help-seeking during AI-supported mathematics learning
examples: Applied to 1,616 chat turns (808 student turns) from 98 Grade-9 students using a web-based Mistral Large tutor on a mathematical-modeling task

article_title: TeachLM: Post-Training LLMs for Education Using Authentic Learning Data
citation: Janos Perczel, Jin Chow, and Dorottya Demszky. (2025). TeachLM: Post-Training LLMs for Education Using Authentic Learning Data. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05087
title: Pipeline for transcribing, diarizing, and cleaning single-track tutoring audio into post-training dialogue data
description: A multi-step data pipeline that converts dual-track Zoom recordings of tutoring sessions into polished tutor-student transcripts suitable for text-based fine-tuning. Audio is merged and trimmed, transcribed with ElevenLabs' API, diarized using per-speaker activity masks, and cleaned with a reasoning model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) through punctuation normalization, backchannel removal, anonymization, and coherence smoothing with enforced turn-taking, followed by human spot checks.
requirements: Dual-track Zoom recordings with separate tracks per speaker for reliable diarization
Human spot checks to ensure transcripts meet the quality bar for post-training
constraints: The article notes prior work shows quality outweighs quantity during fine-tuning, motivating the multi-step cleaning
target_learners: Developers post-training LLMs on conversational learning data
target_learning_goals: Producing high-quality dialogical training data from authentic tutoring sessions
examples: Multiple transcript candidates are generated and the best is selected using Gemini 2.5 Pro to mitigate rare ASR lapses such as dropped segments

article_title: The Tutoring Effectiveness Index: Predicting LLM Math Tutor Quality from Four Conversation Signals
citation: Shim Jaechang and Unggi Lee. 2026. The Tutoring Effectiveness Index: Predicting LLM Math Tutor Quality from Four Conversation Signals. In Proceedings of The 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30666
title: Tutoring Effectiveness Index (TEI): a training-free, judge-free four-signal index for scoring candidate tutor responses
description: TEI is a fixed-weight linear index over four signals computed without any external model at selection time: "a Schoenfeld-Verify keyword ratio, a math-step density, an ends-question rate, and a deep-reasoning gate from the Deep-Thinking Ratio (DTR) probe". Verification and explicit math content are rewarded, ending tutor turns with questions is penalised, and the DTR gate adds a small bonus. Weights (α, β, γ, δ) = (1.0, 0.75, 1.0, 0.5) are fixed a priori from theory to preserve the training-free, judge-free property.
requirements: Runs on a frozen reasoning LLM that exposes explicit thinking traces, enabling per-token DTR computation via forward hooks
constraints: The four weights are fixed a priori from theory; domain calibration could improve performance at the cost of re-introducing a labelled-outcome requirement
The Schoenfeld V signal is regex-derived and surface-level; a GPT-4o-mini paragraph classifier disagrees with it on more than half of paragraphs
All experiments are in mathematics, so TEI weights and signals may need re-derivation for other subjects
target_learners: students tutored by LLM math tutors (simulated GPT-4o-mini student in the evaluation)
target_learning_goals: improving math problem-solving success in multi-turn LLM tutoring dialogues
examples: TEI@8 uses 4.1× the tokens of greedy decoding (16,334 vs. 3,984) and roughly half the cost of Cons@8 (31,868)
key_sources: Shim Jaechang and Unggi Lee. 2026. The Tutoring Effectiveness Index: Predicting LLM Math Tutor Quality from Four Conversation Signals. In Proceedings of The 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30666

article_title: TurtleAI: Benchmarking Multimodal Models for Visual Programming in Turtle Graphics
citation: Chao Wen, Jacqueline Staub, and Adish Singla. (2026). TURTLEAI: Benchmarking Multimodal Models for Visual Programming in Turtle Graphics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03626
title: TURTLEAI benchmark: 823 Turtle Graphics visual programming tasks with datasets, evaluation framework, and data generation technique
description: TURTLEAI is a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on education-oriented visual programming in Turtle Graphics, comprising "(i) TURTLEAI-DS, a collection of evaluation datasets; (ii) TURTLEAI- Eval, an evaluation framework for assessing the correctness of synthesized code; and (iii) TURTLEAI-Datagen, a data generation technique". It contains 823 tasks curated from XLogoOnline tasks used by students in grades 3-6, organized into DSReal (102 real-world tasks), DSCraft (102 hand-drawn renderings), and DSSyn (619 synthetic tasks), across six task categories and three difficulty levels. TURTLEAI-Eval canonicalizes drawings to achieve invariance to translation, scale, and line width before symbolic or embedding-based comparison, with 99.1% and 98.1% agreement with human judgments respectively. The benchmark is publicly released for further research.
requirements: Tasks require generating Python code as a function draw(t) that replicates a target image and satisfies the text-based instruction
constraints: The evaluation framework's normalization step makes comparison invariant to size, translation, and line width, which the authors note may discard meaningful geometric variations essential in inverse graphics tasks
target_learners: students in grades 3-6 learning programming via Turtle Graphics
researchers evaluating vision-language models on educational visual programming
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
programming concepts such as loops, conditionals, and geometric transformations
examples: DSReal tasks were curated from the Midi and Maxi levels of XLogoOnline, with manually written and verified Python reference solutions
Thresholds for the evaluation framework were selected by maximizing agreement with human judgments
key_sources: Chao Wen, Jacqueline Staub, and Adish Singla. (2026). TURTLEAI: Benchmarking Multimodal Models for Visual Programming in Turtle Graphics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03626

article_title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
citation: David Barron, Xiaohang Tang, Rezky Dwisantika, Minsun Kim, David H. Smith IV, Jiaming Cui, and Yan Chen. 2026. TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26184
title: TutorTrace dataset of IDE telemetry, behavioral segments, and observable metrics from 480 learners across four introductory Python deployments
description: TutorTrace is a publicly available dataset from a task-based IDE platform with LLM support, capturing "approximately 180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics" surrounding 1,386 AI interactions across four deployments in two introductory Python courses (N=480). It uniquely combines raw IDE telemetry, AI query and response logs, task outcome data, and expert-validated behavioral classification (Table 1). The dataset, taxonomy, classifier, and code are released via a GitHub repository.
requirements: A task-based IDE environment constraining student activity to a well-defined interaction space so fine-grained behavioral observation is feasible and reproducible
constraints: Data were collected during short introductory programming tasks at a single institution, limiting generalizability across courses, tasks, populations, and learning environments
target_learners: introductory Python programming students in higher education
target_learning_goals: programming problem-solving behavior around AI-assisted help-seeking
examples: Deployments 1–2 used a list-indexing task with a 15-minute limit; Deployments 3–4 used a nested-lists task with a 10-minute limit
key_sources: David Barron, Xiaohang Tang, Rezky Dwisantika, Minsun Kim, David H. Smith IV, Jiaming Cui, and Yan Chen. 2026. TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26184

article_title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
citation: David Barron, Xiaohang Tang, Rezky Dwisantika, Minsun Kim, David H. Smith IV, Jiaming Cui, and Yan Chen. 2026. TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26184
title: TutorTrace three-window behavioral taxonomy of ten learner profiles around AI help-seeking
description: The taxonomy organizes learner activity surrounding AI help-seeking into three temporal windows: before the first AI query (Cold Start, Oriented, Struggling), between consecutive queries (Passive, Iterating, Debugging, Spinning), and session-wide re-querying patterns (Passive Re-querying, Active Testing, Untested Editing) — ten profiles in total. Profiles were derived via outcome-guided K-means clustering over window-specific metric pools, with rule-defined profiles for zero-effort observations. Each profile carries an expert-informed intervention strategy supplied to the AI tutor's prompt, e.g. Cold Start: "Scaffold task entry. Offer pseudocode with blanks."
requirements: Behavioral abstraction pipeline computing observable metrics and behavioral sequences in real time from IDE telemetry
constraints: Window 1 and 2 profiles were selected through an exploratory procedure partly informed by task-completion differences; completion rates are descriptive, not independent validation
target_learners: introductory Python programming students using AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: productive, guided help-seeking and independent effort between AI queries
examples: Window 3 clustering at K=3 (silhouette 0.399) produced assignments identical across 20 random seeds (ARI=1.000)

article_title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
citation: David Barron, Xiaohang Tang, Rezky Dwisantika, Minsun Kim, David H. Smith IV, Jiaming Cui, and Yan Chen. 2026. TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26184
title: TutorTrace automated behavioral classifier transforming raw IDE telemetry into labeled behavioral sequences in real time
description: The TutorTrace classifier is an automated pipeline that transforms raw IDE telemetry into labeled behavioral sequences in real time. Its rules are grounded in the judgment of four domain-expert annotators who coded session replays with a codebook of behaviors such as Implementing, Debugging, Thinking, and Seeking Help, refined over 10 pilot sessions. Validation triangulated learner self-reports, expert annotations, and the automated classifier: "overall Cohen's𝜅 ranged from 0.73 to 0.83, and overall raw agreement ranged from 78% to 87%" (Table 4).
requirements: Expert-developed codebook and consensus segment boundaries derived from manual annotation of session replays; telemetry captured at 37 event types across six source regions
constraints: The rule-based auto-segmentation pipeline lacks semantic understanding of learner code and intent; for example it may classify edits as Debugging while an unresolved error remains even when the learner is implementing an unrelated feature
target_learners: introductory Python programming students whose sessions are classified

citation: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, and Dora Demszky. (2025). Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise. arXiv:2410.03017v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03017v2

description: Tutor CoPilot is a Human-AI system embedded in a virtual tutoring platform (problem display, shared whiteboard, chat window) as "a new Tutor CoPilot button" tutors activate during sessions. An agent guiding students through three-dimensional anatomical structures via natural dialogue

foreign nationals learning Turkish

citation: Popov V, Rochlen LR. (2025). From communication to action: using ordered network analysis to model team performance in clinical simulation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07062-5
title: TuRBO (Team Reflection Behavioral Observation) coding framework adapted with an implementation category
description: TuRBO is a structured observation framework for in-action team reflection in acute care teams, adapted in this study from Schmutz et al. title: Interprofessional death simulation course with unexpected death via advance directive and extended debriefing
description: An interprofessional, simulation-based course ("Training Interprofessional Teams for Daily Clinical Practice and Emergencies") at the TUM Medical Training Center consisting of "five sessions with a duration of 3 to 3.5 h per session" over two and a half weeks. Its fourth session confronted participants with an unexpected death: after about five minutes of unsuccessful resuscitation a trainer delivered the patient's advance directive, and participants stopped resuscitation. Third-year nursing trainees
target_learning_goals: Teamwork and communication skills in clinical and emergency situations
Dealing with termination of resuscitation and patient death
Self-care and reflection after experiencing a patient's death

citation: Celebi N, Griewatz J, Ilg M, Zipfel S, Riessen R, Hoffmann T, Malek NP, Pauluschke-Fröhlich J, Debove I, Muller R, Fröhlich E. (2019). GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(6):Doc77. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001285.shtml
title: Medical faculties implementing faculty-wide basic ultrasound training can choose the tutor-training format that best fits their local conditions
description: Because tutee scanning-skill gains were significant and comparable whether tutors were trained by course, internship, or both, the authors conclude that faculties "can probably train their student-tutors in a way that optimally suits their specific conditions". Each format has stated trade-offs: the course guarantees full curriculum coverage and scales well but limits practice time; the internship offers abundant practice cheaply but risks incomplete topic coverage; the combination carries both advantages and both disadvantages.
requirements: The curriculum should comprise only simple ultrasound skills that can be mastered in a very short timespan, since most students lack extensive supervised laboratory practice
constraints: The finding applies to very simple ultrasound skills; for more complex skills such as echocardiography, tutors trained even three weeks did not match faculty teaching success, as the authors note from prior work
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in faculty-wide mandatory ultrasound courses
target_learning_goals: Basic ultrasound scanning skills
examples: In this study, tutors trained by a course only for one week achieved tutee skill gains comparable to tutors trained four to six weeks by internship or combined routes

article_title: Stress and stressors of medical student near-peer tutors during courses: a psychophysiological mixed methods study.
citation: Hundertmark Jan, Alvarez Simone, Loukanova Svetla, Schultz Jobst-Hendrik. (2019). Stress and stressors of medical student near-peer tutors during courses: a psychophysiological mixed methods study. BMC Medical Education 19:95. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1521-2
title: Taxonomy of near-peer tutors' course-specific and everyday stressors from inductive content analysis
description: Through inductive content analysis of tutors' written free-entry reports, the article builds three category systems: stressors during AaLplus courses, during sonography courses, and general everyday life stressors. Shared course stressors were "time pressure, leadership role demands, uncertainties in medical knowledge, as well as single participants’ characteristics", with time pressure more prevalent in sonography and leadership role demands in AaLplus. Everyday stressors centred on studying for exams, teaching and preparation, doctorate work, and part-time jobs. The taxonomy serves as a basis for designing tutor training and stress prevention.
requirements: Tutors' written reports of stressors experienced in sessions and everyday life, coded into inductive category systems by content analysis
constraints: Qualitative analyses are interpretative by nature; only one author performed the analyses, and other programmes may produce different stressors and stress profiles
target_learners: medical student near-peer tutors
target_learning_goals: peer teaching competence
tutor qualification training
stress prevention in peer-teaching programmes
examples: After 41 (38%) AaLplus sessions and 23 (32%) sonography sessions, tutors reported no stressors; everyday stressors were dominated by studies and exams (29 mentions) and teaching and preparation (18 mentions)
